channel.title: AstroAlert – what's happening in space
channel.description: A daily updated guide to astronomical and space events: eclipses, conjunctions, meteor showers, rocket launches, aurorae and close approaches of asteroids.

item.title: Geminids meteor shower peak
item.description:
14.12.2027, 02:00 UTC

The richest shower of the year and the only major one born not from a comet but from asteroid 3200 Phaethon. Its meteors are slow and often colourful. At maximum, up to 150 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Gemini. Unfortunately the Moon will be 100% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Asteroid 2014 XQ3 passes by
item.description:
12.11.2026, 03:05 UTC

An asteroid with an estimated diameter of 323–721 m will pass Earth at 39.45 million km, or 102.6 times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at 15.7 km/s. For scale: an object of this scale is a heavyweight in the catalogue of near-Earth asteroids. This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. The pass is entirely safe – approaches like this happen regularly and are tracked as a matter of routine.

item.title: Falcon 9 Block 5 | CHORUS
item.description:
31.12.2026, 00:00 UTC

Launch of Falcon 9 Block 5, operated by SpaceX. Site: Cape Canaveral SFS, FL, USA. Schedule status: date to be determined. Mission: CHORUS is MDA's next generation Earth observation constellation, consisting of 2 radar satellites (C-band SAR and X-band SAR), in a 53.5 degree 600 km altitude LEO, with the X-band trailing the C-band by 60 minutes. A collaborative multi-sensor constellation, CHORUS will bring together diverse and unique imagery and data sources and provide a new level of near real-time insight and innovative Earth observation services. Operating in a unique mid-inclination orbit, CHORUS will be able to image day or night, regardless of weather conditions, with daily access of up to 95% of the coverage area. From an industry-leading 700km-wide imaging swath down to sub-metre high resolution, CHORUS will provide the most extensive and unrivalled Earth observation radar imaging capacity available on the market in a single mission. Launch dates slip often – check the current status before tuning into a webcast.

item.title: Starship | Starlink Group 31-2 (Starship Flight 15)
item.description:
13.11.2026, 22:45 UTC

Launch of Starship V3, operated by SpaceX. Site: SpaceX Starbase, TX, USA. Schedule status: date to be confirmed. Mission: 15th test flight of the two-stage Starship launch vehicle and 4th flight of Starship V3. Second Starship flight to deploy satellites (a group of Starlink satellites known as Starlink Group 31-2) into stable Low Earth Orbit and first ever to attempt returning the Starship 2nd stage back to the launch site. The ship is expected to fly at an altitude approximately 275 km above Earth and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet for more than 22 hours, with the ship expected to attempt returning back to Starbase, Texas on its launch pad by pad arms catching. The booster’s primary test objective on Flight 15 will be executing a successful launch, ascent, stage separation, boostback burn, and landing by pad arms catching. This will also be the 1st Starship V3 booster to attempt returning to its launch site. Starship will deliver 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit for the second time, which aim to greatly expand the network's capacity and user speeds. Each Starlink V3 satellite will add 1 Tbps of capacity to the constellation. 3 of the satellites have been modified with a suite of cameras to scan Starship’s heatshield and transmit imagery down to operators. item.title: Leonids meteor shower peak
item.description:
17.11.2027, 02:00 UTC

A shower that roughly every 33 years erupts into a storm with thousands of meteors an hour. In ordinary years it is quiet. At maximum, up to 15 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Leo. Unfortunately the Moon will be 89% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.description:
05.11.2027, 02:00 UTC

At maximum, up to 5 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Taurus. A Moon 38% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.
